## At a glance

Model Project Constructor is a six-step, agent-mediated pipeline that takes a claims-organisation stakeholder's model idea from an unstructured business notion through a guided intake interview, data collection and validation, and an initial GitLab or GitHub project the data-science team can pick up. The business case for it is real and increasingly well evidenced: the pipeline now produces a complete, auditable value story before a model is built (see `executive-summaries/business-value-capture.qmd`), it has been proven end-to-end against a live GitLab host across three internal engineering smoke tests, and it has sustained roughly 3.5 months of dated, test-gated commit velocity — 384 commits, 971 tests, 97.75% coverage — with recent priorities aimed squarely at clearing the path to an enterprise deployment. What the evidence does not yet show is adoption by an actual claims team on a real business idea; the three live pilot projects are the engineering team's own scripted runs of the same demonstration scenario, not validated production use.

The legal posture is largely resolved and well documented. The repository's own licensing (MIT), its dependency tree (zero GPL/AGPL/LGPL, three low-risk MPL-2.0 transitive components), its third-party methodology attribution, and its AI-co-authorship disclosure are all consistent, current, and independently reverified this session. One decision remains genuinely open and belongs to Legal — the intellectual-property disposition of the codebase (assignment, work-for-hire, or third-party open-source-software intake) — and it has been deliberately deferred to run after the fork, inside the enterprise clone, rather than resolved here. Two narrower gaps this document first surfaced — the pipeline's generated-project output carrying no license, and the published wiki carrying no license of its own — were both closed in Session 197 (see Legal safety, "Resolved").

Enterprise-environment readiness is mixed by design, not by neglect: the project's data-source-inventory architecture, its SQL quality-check execution, and its AWS Bedrock client migration are all genuinely built and tested, and several security hardening items (SECURITY.md, dependency-license removal, secret-scanning) have shipped recently. But real gaps remain and should not be minimized: the intake web UI has no authentication or CSRF protection, a misconfigured deployment can silently create projects against the public GitLab.com instead of an intended private instance, CI lacks dependency-update automation and supply-chain pinning, and Bedrock support has never had a live model call succeed against a real enterprise AWS account. **Recommendation**: proceed to the enterprise-clone fork — its own gate (Phases A1–A4, B1's core, and B2) is independently satisfied and does not depend on this document — while carrying forward, with named owners, the open items catalogued in Sections 3–5 below. This document does not itself resolve or gate anything; it is a synthesis for the people who need the full picture before and around that decision.

## Business benefit

### What the pipeline does and for whom

The pipeline compresses a process that today runs on narrative and intuition — a claims-org stakeholder's model idea, developed through ad hoc conversations and unstructured handoffs — into a structured, six-step flow with a defined schema at every handoff. A business stakeholder visits an intake portal with a model idea; an Intake Agent conducts a guided interview (up to 20 questions) converging on the business problem, proposed solution, model solution, and estimated value; a Data Agent turns that report into SQL for data collection, quality-check queries, and validated data; a Website Agent produces a GitLab or GitHub project containing a draft Business Understanding, an Implementation Plan, a Data section with query explanation and exploratory analysis, and an initial model build and evaluation; and the data-science team inherits a working scaffold rather than a set of meeting notes. The canonical worked example throughout the project's history — a subrogation-recovery scenario, where adjusters under a new claims system are failing to capture the evidence needed to pursue recovery — illustrates the shape of problem this is built for, not a single case it solves.

This serves three audiences: claims-org business stakeholders who need a structured, fundable path from idea to proposal; the data-science team, who receives a repository with EDA, initial models, and governance already drafted instead of an unstructured handoff; and, more broadly, data analysts, since the Data Agent ships as an installable, standalone Python package (`packages/data-agent`) with its own CLI, usage documentation, and an architecturally enforced decoupling boundary from the intake schema, verified by a dedicated CI test. No evidence was found that any analyst team has adopted the standalone package yet, and its PyPI distribution step has not happened — this is a shipped, enforced *capability* for reuse, not yet reuse that has occurred.

### The value-capture capability

Beyond producing a scaffold, the pipeline now produces the business case itself, before a model is built, and a measurement plan that survives the handoff into production — the intake interview converges on a value-measurement plan (baseline metric, counterfactual design, attribution method, evaluation horizon, review cadence, success criteria, decision rights) alongside the original business case, and the data agent executes SQL to record that baseline before training begins. This capability is documented in full, with a worked example, in `executive-summaries/business-value-capture.qmd`; it shipped across six coordinated changes in Sessions 85–93 (May 2026), confirmed against `CHANGELOG.md`. It is not re-narrated here — the relevant point for this dossier is that it materially strengthens the funding case a sponsor sees at each stage of a model's life cycle: a defensible business case at funding, a pre-declared measurement plan at deployment, and a single auditable number at review.

### Evidence of real-world traction — and its limits

Three GitLab projects exist as live proof the pipeline works end-to-end against a real repository host: `subrogation-pilot`, `subrogation-pilot-v2`, and `subrogation-pilot-v3`, created across Sessions 22, 24, and 26–27 respectively as the engineering team progressively turned on the pipeline's real (non-mocked) components — first the website-generation and repo-creation machinery, then the real LLM-backed Data Agent, then the real Intake Agent via a scripted-answers fixture. All three runs use the same subrogation scenario as the standing smoke-test fixture, auto-suffixed `-v2`/`-v3` only because of a GitLab project-name collision, not because three distinct business ideas were run. This is meaningful evidence that the pipeline mechanics work end-to-end with real infrastructure and, for two of three stages, real LLM calls — it is not evidence that any claims-org team has used the tool on its own idea, and no model was trained or deployed against real claims data in any of the three runs. The three projects' own future disposition — leave as-is under the personal GitLab namespace, or migrate into the enterprise clone — is recorded elsewhere as genuinely undecided, consistent with their status as internal test artifacts rather than committed business assets.

### Development velocity

The repository shows 384 commits spanning roughly 110 days (first commit 2026-04-10, most recent 2026-07-28, the date of this document), with 971 tests collected live this session — reconciling exactly against the most recently reported 963 passed plus 8 live-skipped at 97.75% coverage. The three most recent shipped changes are the removal of both remaining LGPL-3.0 direct dependencies (`python-gitlab` and `PyGithub`, replaced with direct HTTP calls) and the AWS Bedrock client migration to Bedrock-native authentication — work explicitly aimed at enterprise readiness rather than unrelated feature development. This is sustained, dated, test-gated investment, and its recent direction is pointed at the same enterprise transition this dossier is written for.

## Legal safety

### Resolved

The repository's own license is consistent across all points of reference — `LICENSE`, both `pyproject.toml` files, and `README.md` all agree on MIT, copyright R. Mark Sharp, with no drift from a previously flagged inconsistency. The dependency tree carries zero GPL, AGPL, or LGPL licenses of any kind, direct or transitive — independently reverified this session by grepping the lockfile and both package manifests — following the removal of the project's two former LGPL dependencies. Three MPL-2.0 transitive components remain (`certifi`, `orjson`, `pathspec`); MPL-2.0 is a file-level weak-copyleft license that imposes no obligation here because the project does not modify those packages' source, and is standard, low-risk territory commonly bundled alongside permissive stacks.

The project's third-party methodology material — `SESSION_RUNNER.md`, `SAFEGUARDS.md`, the `docs/methodology/` files, and related seed content — originates from Terrell Deppe's "Iterative Session Methodology" and is used here under a documented permission grant (MIT-style use and redistribution), recorded in the repository's `NOTICE` file. `NOTICE` is explicit that it documents the grant's existence and terms as relayed to the project rather than being the grant itself, and that continued use is contingent on that permission holding — a live dependency on an external party's goodwill, but a currently well-documented one. AI-provenance disclosure is likewise in place: `NOTICE` discloses substantial Claude-assisted development, and the figure was reverified live this session at 358 of 384 commits (93.2%) carrying a Claude co-authorship trailer, materially unchanged from the prior snapshot. The copyright holder of record is a single individual, which simplifies matters procedurally, though it does not by itself resolve the open item below. The core legal-hygiene artifact set — `LICENSE`, `NOTICE`, `SECURITY.md`, `CODEOWNERS`, `THIRD-PARTY-LICENSES`, `CONTRIBUTING.md` — is present and current as of this session.

**Resolved since this dossier's original session (Session 197):** the two narrower gaps this document itself first surfaced —

- **The pipeline's generated-project output now carries a license placeholder.** The website-generation agent's base scaffold (`templates.py`) now emits a `LICENSE` file for every generated project — a proprietary/confidential placeholder naming the requesting stakeholder and scaffold date, explicit that no terms have been confirmed by Legal, with a pointer from the generated `README.md`. This closes the "ships with no license declaration at all" gap; it does not itself decide what license terms downstream projects should ultimately carry — that remains Legal's call — it stops the pipeline from silently emitting zero declaration in the meantime.
- **The published wiki now states its own license.** `docs/wiki/claims-model-starter/License.md` (linked from `_Sidebar.md` and `Home.md`) states the same MIT terms as this repository's own `LICENSE`, closing item 4 of `enterprise-migration.md` §2.7's "Four legal items." This does not change the wiki's *disposition* — D6 already settled that the wiki stays public indefinitely (§1.2) — only what terms now govern its content.

### Open

One item remains genuinely open and should be represented to reviewers as such, not as resolved:

- **IP disposition (decision D3)** — whether the codebase's intellectual property should be treated as assignment, work-for-hire, or third-party open-source-software intake — is Legal's decision and has not been resolved in this repository. The migration plan's own recommendation is to default to third-party OSS intake, but its timing was deliberately moved (Session 190) to run **after** the enterprise fork, inside the clone, rather than pre-fork. This dossier should not be read as closing D3.

Artifacts tied to unresolved downstream decisions — a machine-readable license manifest (`REUSE.toml`), and a contributor license agreement or developer certificate of origin mechanism — remain absent, consistent with those decisions (D3 and the corporate-host DCO/CLA question, D4) not yet being answered.

## Enterprise-environment readiness

### Security

Several hardening items have shipped recently and should be credited: `SECURITY.md` documents a private-disclosure process; a `.gitleaksignore` is in place; a live secret-scan of the full git history (386 commits) returned no leaks. Real gaps remain, though. The intake web UI has no authentication, authorization, or CSRF protection on any route, and no explicit cross-origin policy — anyone who can reach the web port can start, read, and drive interview sessions; this is an intranet-trust-boundary design today, not one with its own access-control layer. A deployment that omits the host-URL configuration flag will silently create projects against the public `gitlab.com` (or `api.github.com`) rather than an intended private enterprise instance, with no error raised. TLS verification defaults safely to on, but there is no supported way to point it at a custom internal certificate authority without a code change, which matters behind a TLS-inspecting enterprise proxy. Local session and checkpoint stores are plaintext and world-readable on a shared host, though correctly excluded from the git repository itself. The intake UI still loads its JavaScript framework from a public CDN — now integrity-hash-protected against tampering, but still a network dependency that would fail closed on a locked-down enterprise network. CI has no automated dependency updates, static-analysis security scanning, license gating, or software-bill-of-materials generation.

### Testing

Test count and coverage are current and undrifted as of this session: 971 tests collected (963 passing, 8 intentionally live-skipped) at 97.75% coverage, matching the most recently reported baseline exactly, with the latest commit touching only planning and audit documents rather than source or test code. The CI workflow itself has three structural weaknesses relevant to an enterprise migration: third-party GitHub Actions are pinned to floating major-version tags rather than fixed commits, dependency installation does not enforce the committed lockfile, and all jobs run only on GitHub-hosted runners with no path for enterprise-controlled or network-restricted runners. None of these affect current test correctness, but all three matter for supply-chain integrity and runner-residency control in an enterprise CI environment.

### Data readiness

The data-source architecture is more built than a cautious assumption would suggest. A formal contract defining multiple producer types (curated, automated, interview, external-catalog) is implemented and validated; an automated producer that reflects live PostgreSQL and SQLite schemas via `information_schema` introspection is implemented, tested, and wired into a real CLI command with an optional LLM-assisted ranking step; the curated producer is schema-only by deliberate design (no code is needed to support a hand-supplied inventory); and the consumer side — the data agent's query-generation prompt — actually incorporates whichever inventory is supplied, with provenance tracked back to the source. SQL quality-check execution against a connected database is real and functioning, with parse-level validation as a first gate and live execution as the semantic gate.

Two producer types are architecturally supported but not built: an interview-sourced producer (converting intake question-and-answer pairs into inventory entries) and an external-catalog producer. Both are explicitly and deliberately deferred as design choices rather than oversights — the project's own planning documents frame the interview-sourced producer as something that "may stay unimplemented indefinitely" absent pilot demand — and neither appears as scheduled work in the active backlog. This should be represented plainly rather than smoothed over: three of four producer classes are real and load-bearing today; two classes remain unbuilt by design.

### Bedrock readiness

The migration to Bedrock-native authentication (`AnthropicBedrockMantle`, replacing the older SigV4-only client) is complete and merged in both places the client exists. Enterprise-networking pass-throughs — a private-endpoint host override, a custom HTTP client for TLS inspection or proxying, and a guard against a stray bearer token silently bypassing role-based authentication — are all implemented in the client code, but none of them are yet wired into the application's production configuration surface; this is a tracked open decision (below), not a code defect.

Several decisions remain genuinely open and gate different downstream phases: whether the Bedrock endpoint should be regional or global (a data-residency question), how to wire the implemented networking pass-throughs into live configuration, and whether named AWS SSO profile support is needed — none of these are resolved in code today. An IAM trust-policy artifact has been deliberately carved out and deferred to run after the fork, inside the enterprise clone, and is not this repository's problem to close. Most importantly, live end-to-end validation has never succeeded: authentication, endpoint resolution, and region resolution have been confirmed live, but every attempted live model call returned an account-eligibility error, and a subsequent AWS quota-increase request was denied. Bedrock support is implemented, merged, and unit-tested — it has not been proven to work end-to-end against a real account, and stakeholders should be told this plainly rather than have it implied away. A further unresolved branch exists in the deployment documentation: three yes/no security questions posed to the target enterprise account's security team (mandatory guardrails, mandatory FIPS compliance, existing model-runtime quota) that, if answered "yes" on either of the first two, would force a materially different and currently unbuilt integration path.

## Where this stands

This dossier is pre-fork groundwork produced per `docs/planning/enterprise-migration.md`'s "New (pre-fork)" backlog item — a stakeholder-, legal-, and security-facing synthesis of the pipeline's business case, legal posture, and enterprise readiness, requested by the operator ahead of the enterprise-clone fork. It does not itself gate or unblock any phase of that migration: Phase C4's actual gate — Phases A1–A4 complete, Phase B1's D3-independent core complete, and Phase B2 complete — is independently satisfied as of this session's starting commit, regardless of this document's existence or content. Its purpose is to give reviewers outside the engineering team a single, honest place to read the full picture — including the items above that remain genuinely open — before and around that decision, not to certify it.
